e.etymology: From Greek Zenon, a name derived from Zeus. Two philosophers made it famous: Zeno of Elea, who posed the paradoxes of motion, and Zeno of Citium, the founder of Stoicism.
namesakes: Zeno of Elea (Greek philosopher of the paradoxes)
Zeno of Citium (founder of Stoic philosophy)

assoc.t: Zeno's paradoxes, such as Achilles and the tortoise
Zeno, the childlike Omni-King of Dragon Ball Super

e.etymology: A respelling of Grayson, an English surname meaning son of the grieve, a Middle English word for a steward or bailiff.
From Hebrew even ha-ezer, stone of help, the name Samuel gives a memorial stone in 1 Samuel. Puritans took it up as a given name in the 17th century.

assoc.t: Ebenezer Scrooge, the miser of A Christmas Carol

e.note: Closely tied to Ebenezer Scrooge, so the name can read as miserly or old-fashioned.

e.etymology: From Arabic iman, faith or belief, from the verb amana, to believe. The spelling with a double a is common in South Asian families, where it reached Urdu and Punjabi through Persian.
Several sources share this spelling: the common Japanese surname Kato, the Luganda name for the younger of twin boys in Uganda, and a K spelling of the Roman name Cato.
namesakes: Kato Kaelin (houseguest witness in the O.J. Simpson trial)

assoc.t: the Green Hornet's sidekick, once played by Bruce Lee

e.etymology: A trimmed spelling of Adeline, the Old French pet form of Adela that the Normans brought to England, from Germanic adal, noble.

A respelling of Cataleya, the Spanish name of the cattleya orchid, a flower named for English horticulturist William Cattley. The name took off after the 2011 film Colombiana, whose heroine is called Cataleya.
A modern Indian name glossed as unique, built on Sanskrit a-, not, and dvi, two: one without a second.
A pet form of Olivia, from Latin oliva, olive. Livy is also the English name of the Roman historian Titus Livius.

assoc.t: Livy, Roman historian of the age of Augustus

e.etymology: A respelling of Renesmee, the name Stephenie Meyer coined in Breaking Dawn, the last Twilight novel, for Bella and Edward's daughter. It joins Renée and Esme, the names of the child's grandmothers.

assoc.t: Renesmee, Bella and Edward's daughter in Twilight

e.etymology: Taken from Broly, the Legendary Super Saiyan of the Dragon Ball films. Like other Saiyan names it is a vegetable pun, here on broccoli. US use rose with the film Dragon Ball Super: Broly (2018).

assoc.t: Broly, the Legendary Super Saiyan of Dragon Ball

e.meaning: ginger, the spice; also a pet form of Virginia
e.etymology: Began as a pet form of Virginia and as a nickname for redheads, from the spice word ginger. Dancer and actress Ginger Rogers, born Virginia McMath, made it familiar in the 1930s.
namesakes: Ginger Rogers (Fred Astaire's dance partner and Oscar-winning actress)

assoc.t: ginger, the spice and root
a ginger, a red-haired person
Ginger, the movie star on Gilligan's Island
Ginger Spice, Geri Halliwell of the Spice Girls

e.note: Ginger is everyday slang for a redhead, sometimes used as a tease.

e.etymology: The English word gauge, a measure or measuring instrument, from Old North French gauge. As a name it is a spelling of Gage, a surname for an official who checked weights and measures.

assoc.t: gauge, a measuring dial, as in fuel gauge
shotgun bore size, as in 12-gauge
gauges, stretched ear piercings

e.etymology: Two unrelated sources: the Roman family name of the Stoic philosopher Seneca, likely from Latin senex, old, and the Seneca Nation of the Iroquois, whose English name comes from a Dutch form of an Algonquian word.
namesakes: Seneca Crane (head gamemaker in The Hunger Games)

assoc.t: Seneca, Roman Stoic philosopher and tutor of Nero
Seneca Nation, one of the six Iroquois nations
Seneca Falls, site of the 1848 women's rights convention

e.etymology: A respelling of Amaya, the Spanish form of Basque Amaia, from amai, end. An 1879 Spanish novel, Amaya, made it a given name; the -iya spelling is American.
The English color word for a greenish blue, one of the four inks of color printing, from Greek kyanos, dark blue.

assoc.t: cyan, the blue-green printer ink, the C in CMYK
Cyan, the samurai of Final Fantasy VI

e.etymology: A respelling of Madelyn, the English form of French Madeleine, from Magdalene, woman of Magdala, a town on the Sea of Galilee whose name means tower.
A respelling of Blaze, the English word for a bright flame, from Old English blæse, torch. Blaze also serves as a phonetic spelling of Blaise, the French form of the Latin name Blasius.

assoc.t: blaze, the everyday word for a fire (same sound)

e.etymology: A feminine form of Cyrus, the Greek and Latin rendering of Old Persian Kurush, the name of the founder of the Persian Empire. The meaning of Kurush is not settled.
From Arabic nur, light. An-Nur, the Light, is one of the names of God in Islam and the title of the 24th sura of the Quran. The name is given to both girls and boys.
From Arabic qamar, moon. Al-Qamar, the Moon, is the 54th sura of the Quran, and the full moon is a classic image of beauty in Arabic poetry.

e.meaning: dignified, or bell, depending on the kanji
e.etymology: A Japanese name for girls and boys whose meaning depends on the character chosen: most often one meaning dignified or bracing, or one meaning bell. It has ranked among Japan's top girls' names in recent years.

assoc.t: name of many anime characters, as in Fate and Naruto

e.etymology: From Sanskrit arha, worthy or deserving, the root behind arhat, the worthy one of Buddhist and Jain tradition. Used mainly by Indian families.
An American name of the 1980s and 90s, shaped like Sierra and Tierra with a K. It is usually treated as a form of Kiara or Kiera, from Irish Ciara, the feminine of Ciarán, little dark one.
namesakes: Kierra Sheard (gospel singer, daughter of Karen Clark Sheard)

e.etymology: A spelling of Jayden, a name American parents coined in the late 20th century by putting J in front of the sound of Aidan, Braden, Caden and Hayden.
namesakes: Jaeden Martell (actor in It and Knives Out)

e.etymology: The Spanish pet form of Guadalupe, by way of Lupe plus -ita. Guadalupe is a Spanish place name from Arabic wadi, river valley, and probably Latin lupus, wolf, honored through Our Lady of Guadalupe.
namesakes: Lupita Nyong'o (Oscar-winning actress in 12 Years a Slave and Black Panther)

assoc.t: Lupita Nyong'o, Oscar-winning actress

e.etymology: A respelling of Erin, the anglicized form of Irish Éirinn, a poetic name for Ireland. For boys it also overlaps with Aaron, which sounds the same in most American accents.
An Irish surname, from Ó Caoinleáin, descendant of Caoindealbhán, a personal name built from caoin, fine or graceful, and dealbh, shape.
A short form of Brianna, the feminine of Brian, an Irish name likely from a Celtic root meaning high or noble. The spelling matches Brie, the French cheese and the region east of Paris it comes from.
namesakes: Brie Larson (Oscar winner for Room and star of Captain Marvel)
Brie Bella (WWE wrestler and reality TV star)

assoc.t: Brie, the soft French cheese

e.note: Spelled like the French cheese, so cheese jokes are likely.

e.etymology: From Latin maris, of the sea, taken from Stella Maris, star of the sea, a title of the Virgin Mary. Separately it is a short form of Maria in Estonia and a men's name, Māris, in Latvia.

assoc.t: Roger Maris, Yankee who hit 61 home runs in 1961
Maris Crane, Niles's never-seen wife on Frasier

e.meaning: son of Aodh, a Gaelic name meaning fire
e.etymology: A Scottish and Irish surname, from Gaelic MacAoidh, son of Aodh, a name meaning fire. As a first name it is most used among Latter-day Saints, in honor of church president David O. McKay.
A respelling of Kaden or Caden, one of the rhyming -aden names (Aiden, Braden, Jayden) that swept the US in the 2000s. Caden is sometimes linked to the Irish surname McCadden.
